title: Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator: $25,000+ Funding, Mentorship and Global Support for Early-Stage Tech Nonprofits
summary: The Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is an opportunity for early-stage technology nonprofits using innovative digital solutions to address major social, environmental, health, education, economic, or humanitarian challenges. The programme is designed to help promising tech nonprofits strengthen their organizations, improve their technology and products, access philanthropic capital, develop sustainable growth strategies, and connect with a powerful global community of founders, funders, technology professionals, and social-impact leaders. Applications for the 2027 cohort open on August 17, 2026 , and close on September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT) . Fast Forward describes itself as an organization focused on helping entrepreneurs apply the best of technology to some of the world s biggest social problems. Through its Accelerator and wider ecosystem of resources, the organization brings together the technology, nonprofit, and philanthropic sectors to help technology-driven nonprofits move from early-stage development toward sustainable scale. According to Fast Forward, it has accelerated 112+ tech nonprofits , which have collectively gone on to impact more than 415 million lives and raise more than $1.4 billion in follow-on funding . About the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator The Fast Forward Accelerator is the organization s flagship and longest-standing programme for early-stage tech nonprofits. Rather than functioning simply as a conventional grant programme, the Accelerator combines philanthropic funding, training, mentorship, community, strategic guidance, fundraising support, product development expertise, and visibility . The programme is specifically designed around the challenges faced by organizations that operate at the intersection of technology and social impact. Selected organizations receive a combination of: $25,000+ in philanthropic seed capital Tailored training and educational content Mentorship and expert guidance Access to a community of technology nonprofit founders Support with fundraising and nonprofit development Product and technology guidance Growth and scaling strategies Opportunities to connect with funders and supporters Exposure through Fast Forward s broader ecosystem Participation in Demo Days attended by a large audience of funders and supporters The programme aims to select approximately 10 teams per cohort , although Fast Forward notes that the exact number can fluctuate depending on the strength and composition of the applicant pool. What Is a Tech Nonprofit? A central requirement for this opportunity is that applicants operate as technology nonprofits. Fast Forward defines a tech nonprofit as a nonprofit organization that uses technology, including artificial intelligence, to address challenges affecting people, communities, society, or humanity more broadly. Examples can include organizations working in areas such as: Healthcare access Education and education equity Climate action Humanitarian assistance Poverty reduction Digital inclusion Public-interest technology Economic opportunity Community development Social justice Accessibility Environmental sustainability Civic participation Other major social or humanitarian challenges The defining characteristic is that technology is central to the organization s solution and social impact model . Fast Forward points to organizations such as Wikipedia and Khan Academy as examples of technology nonprofits and notes that its directory included more than 1,400 tech nonprofits worldwide as of 2026. What Support Does the Accelerator Provide? The Accelerator is structured around three major areas of support: Capital, Content, and Cohort . 1. Capital Early-stage technology nonprofits often face a difficult funding environment. Traditional nonprofit funders may not understand technology-based business models, while traditional technology investors may not be interested in organizations whose primary objective is social impact rather than financial profit. Fast Forward seeks to help bridge this gap. Participants receive $25,000 or more in seed philanthropic capital , while also gaining guidance on navigating the fundraising environment for technology nonprofits. This funding can provide an important source of early-stage capital as an organization works to strengthen its technology, team, operations, impact measurement, and growth strategy. 2. Content and Training The Accelerator provides curriculum addressing both sides of the technology nonprofit equation. On the nonprofit side, participants may receive guidance related to areas such as: Board development Impact measurement Volunteer management Fundraising Organizational development Nonprofit operations On the technology side, the programme explores topics such as: Product development Go-to-market strategy Technology leadership Scaling Growth Product strategy Sustainable expansion This combination is particularly relevant to founders who have strong technical or social-impact expertise but need support in strengthening the other side of their organization. 3. Cohort and Community Building a technology nonprofit can be challenging because founders often face problems that are different from those encountered by traditional nonprofits or conventional technology startups. The Accelerator therefore places considerable emphasis on peer learning and community. Selected founders become part of a cohort of organizations facing similar challenges. They also become part of Fast Forward s broader portfolio and ecosystem, allowing them to build relationships beyond the immediate programme. This network can provide opportunities for: Peer learning Collaboration Mentorship Knowledge exchange Strategic partnerships Fundraising connections Technology expertise Long-term community support Key Programme Timeline for the 2027 Cohort Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates and programme milestones: Programme Stage Date/Period Application Opens August 17, 2026 Application Workshop August 12, 2026, 10:00–11:00 a.m. PT Application Deadline September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. PT Interviews October–December 2026 Final Notifications By the end of 2026 Programme Begins Late February 2027 Programme Ends Early June 2027 Demo Days Late May–early June 2027 Applicants should prepare their materials well before the deadline because the application requires detailed information about the organization, its technology, its impact, its leadership, and its potential for growth. Application Deadline The application deadline for the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT). Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit. The application process may require coordination between multiple co-founders, preparation of organizational information, development of a compelling narrative, and potentially the creation or submission of video materials. Who Is Fast Forward Looking For? Fast Forward uses a holistic application review process. This means the organization does not evaluate applicants based on a single factor. The organization states that its only hard requirement is that applicants are: Early-stage tech nonprofits with at least a minimum viable product (MVP) built. Beyond this requirement, Fast Forward considers several characteristics when evaluating an organization s fit. Leadership Fast Forward looks for visionary leaders capable of navigating both the technology and nonprofit environments. Strong applicants should be able to demonstrate: A clear vision Strong understanding of the problem being addressed Leadership capability Commitment to social impact Ability to build and lead a team Willingness to learn and adapt Understanding of both technology and organizational development You do not necessarily have to be the original founder to apply. Fast Forward states that the current leader of an organization can apply. Technology Talent The organization values technology expertise within leadership teams. Applicants should ideally have mission-driven technology professionals in leadership positions or a credible plan for bringing appropriate technology talent onto the team. Fast Forward recognizes that hiring a full-time Chief Technology Officer may not be financially realistic for every early-stage organization. Therefore, organizations that outsource some software development are still encouraged to apply when their software is central to their impact. However, having strong internal technology leadership or a clear plan to establish it can strengthen an application. Impact Potential Applicants should demonstrate that their organization has the potential to make a meaningful difference. This involves clearly explaining: What problem the organization addresses Who experiences the problem Why the problem is important How the organization s solution works Why technology is necessary or particularly valuable How many people could ultimately benefit What evidence exists that the solution is working What additional impact could occur if the organization scales Scalability Fast Forward places particular emphasis on software-based solutions with significant growth potential. Applicants should therefore demonstrate that their technology can potentially serve a much larger population without requiring costs to increase at exactly the same rate as users or beneficiaries. A strong application should explain how the organization can move from its current stage toward broader adoption and impact. Lived Experience Fast Forward recognizes the value of founders and leaders who have personally experienced the problem they are trying to solve. Applicants can strengthen their case by explaining relevant lived experience and showing how that experience contributes to their understanding of the community, challenge, or problem. This does not mean every applicant must personally have experienced the problem. Rather, it demonstrates why deep understanding of the people being served is important. Alignment Fast Forward also considers whether its resources, expertise, network, and investment can make a meaningful difference to the organization. Applicants should therefore think carefully about why Fast Forward is the right accelerator for their organization at its current stage. You Do Not Have to Be a Perfect Match One of the notable aspects of Fast Forward s application guidance is its encouragement to organizations that meet most, but not necessarily every, preferred characteristic. The organization specifically encourages applicants not to self-reject simply because they do not perfectly match every criterion. This is particularly important for founders who may underestimate their competitiveness because they lack one desirable characteristic. If your organization meets the fundamental requirement of being an early-stage technology nonprofit with an MVP and has strong potential for social impact, Fast Forward encourages you to consider applying. The Accelerator Is Global The Fast Forward Accelerator is not restricted to organizations based in the United States. The programme is global and Fast Forward states that it prioritizes geographic diversity within its cohorts. Organizations based outside the United States can apply provided they meet the relevant nonprofit requirements. For example, an organization based outside the U.S. does not necessarily need to possess U.S. 501(c)(3) status. Fast Forward states that organizations can apply if they are registered as nonprofits in their own countries . This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to technology nonprofits across Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, the Middle East, Oceania, and other regions. Can Organizations Outside San Francisco Apply? Yes. Applicants do not need to be located in San Francisco or the Bay Area. However, participation requires attendance at certain in-person components of the programme. The Accelerator includes: An in-person kickoff in San Francisco in February In-person and virtual Demo Days in May and/or June Mostly virtual programming throughout the programme Fast Forward provides additional travel support for teams based outside the Bay Area to help facilitate participation in required in-person activities. This means international applicants should be prepared to travel to the United States when required by the programme. Programme Time Commitment Applicants should carefully consider the time commitment before applying. Fast Forward describes the Accelerator as a major commitment . The programme is scheduled for: Tuesdays and Thursdays 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. Pacific Time Approximately three additional meeting hours each week Additional homework and preparation outside scheduled programming At least one co-founder must attend every session . Additionally, the co-founder who will pitch at Demo Day must participate in all relevant pitch practice sessions. This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because the programme schedule is based on Pacific Time. Participants in Africa, Europe, Asia, and other regions should assess the time-zone implications before applying. The Fast Forward Accelerator Is Hybrid The programme combines virtual and in-person participation. Most of the Accelerator s programming takes place virtually, making it accessible to organizations around the world. However, participants should expect in-person components, including: A kickoff in San Francisco in February 2027 In-person components associated with Demo Days Other required in-person programme activities where applicable Fast Forward provides travel assistance for teams located outside the Bay Area. The organization also states that accommodations can be provided for in-person programming weeks, although accommodations are not provided for the entire programme. Demo Days and Investor Exposure One of the major highlights of the Accelerator is Demo Day. Demo Days provide participating organizations with an opportunity to present the progress they have made during the programme to a large audience of funders and supporters. Fast Forward states that Demo Day audiences can include more than 1,000 funders and supporters . For an early-stage technology nonprofit, this can create opportunities for: Visibility Fundraising Strategic partnerships Donor relationships Ecosystem connections Future growth Increased credibility The Demo Day presentation is therefore not simply a final academic exercise. It can serve as an important opportunity for organizations to communicate their mission, demonstrate evidence of impact, present their technology, and explain their future growth strategy to potential supporters. Can an Organization Apply Without Formal U.S. Nonprofit Registration? Yes. Fast Forward states that organizations that are not yet formally registered as nonprofits may still apply, and the organization can provide assistance with the incorporation process. For organizations outside the United States, Fast Forward states that they can apply without a U.S. 501(c)(3) designation as long as they are registered as nonprofits in their own country. This makes the programme more accessible to international nonprofit organizations. Can Organizations Without an MVP Apply? No. Having a minimum viable product (MVP) is the fundamental hard requirement identified by Fast Forward. Organizations that are still at the idea, concept, or research stage are therefore not yet eligible for the Accelerator. However, Fast Forward recommends that early-stage teams without an MVP make use of its technology nonprofit resources and playbooks to develop their ideas toward implementation. This distinction is important: the Accelerator is designed for organizations that have progressed beyond the idea stage and already have a working MVP. What If Software Development Is Outsourced? Organizations that outsource software development can still apply. Fast Forward prefers organizations with internal technology leadership or plans to hire a Chief Technology Officer in the near future, but recognizes that early-stage organizations may not have sufficient resources to maintain a large internal technical team. The key consideration is whether software is central to the organization s impact . Therefore, applicants that rely on external developers should clearly explain: Why technology is central to the mission How the software is developed and maintained Who owns the product and technical vision How technical decisions are made Whether the organization plans to develop internal technical capacity How the technology will scale Additional Resources Available Through Fast Forward The Accelerator is only one component of Fast Forward s wider support ecosystem. Tech Nonprofit Tools Fast Forward provides guides and resources covering areas such as: Scaling Fundraising Product design Revenue Organizational development Technology nonprofit strategy These resources are particularly useful for organizations that are not yet ready for the Accelerator. Tech Nonprofit Directory Fast Forward operates a directory of technology nonprofits designed to increase their visibility among: Funders Potential employees Advisors Partners Other ecosystem stakeholders Being part of a broader technology nonprofit ecosystem can help organizations become more discoverable. Tech Nonprofit Job Board Fast Forward also maintains a job board featuring opportunities from technology nonprofits. Organizations can use the platform to find mission-driven talent, while technology professionals can discover employment opportunities in the social-impact sector. Funding Forward Funding Forward is a weekly newsletter featuring information about: Grant opportunities Events Resources Articles Opportunities relevant to social entrepreneurs For organizations that are not yet ready for the Accelerator, following Fast Forward s funding resources can help them identify future opportunities. What s Good in Tech Fast Forward s monthly What s Good in Tech communication highlights developments within the Fast Forward ecosystem and the broader technology-for-good sector. AI for Humanity The organization also provides a monthly newsletter focused on AI-powered nonprofits and developments in the use of artificial intelligence for social impact. Fast Forward s Broader Areas of Focus Fast Forward s work is organized around several strategic priorities. 1. Building the Pipeline Fast Forward seeks to expand the technology nonprofit sector by supporting a diverse pipeline of high-impact and community-driven builders. 2. Launching Promising Builders The Accelerator serves as the organization s flagship mechanism for supporting promising early-stage technology nonprofit organizations. 3. Supporting Scale Fast Forward also supports nonprofits that have progressed beyond the startup stage and require guidance to become larger and more influential organizations. 4. Strengthening the Ecosystem The organization works with leaders throughout the technology-for-good ecosystem to increase access to capital, resources, expertise, and visibility. 5. Maximizing AI for Social Impact Fast Forward is also focused on helping nonprofits use artificial intelligence to strengthen their missions and increase their potential social impact. Fast Forward s Funding and Partnership Ecosystem Fast Forward is a U.S. 501(c)(3) organization and works with technology companies, philanthropic foundations, and other supporters. Its listed supporters include organizations and foundations such as Google.org, BlackRock, The HPE Foundation, Ballmer Group, Bloomberg, Salesforce, Okta, Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, Twilio.org, ServiceNow, Dell Technologies, Reid Hoffman, Deloitte Health Equity Institute, The William Flora Hewlett Foundation, Splunk, Pinterest, eBay Foundation, The Equinix Foundation, The UPS Foundation, Akamai Foundation, GitLab Foundation, Comcast Business, OpenAI, HubSpot, New Relic, and Docusign, among others. This broader ecosystem is one of the potential advantages for Accelerator participants because the programme connects technology nonprofits with organizations operating across technology, philanthropy, finance, and social impact. Application Process The application process is designed to help Fast Forward understand the organization, its leadership, technology, social problem, and potential for scale. Applicants should expect to provide information about areas such as: The organization and its mission The social problem being addressed The target population The technology or software solution The current MVP Evidence of progress and impact Leadership and team capabilities Technology expertise Growth and scalability Funding and organizational development Future plans Why Fast Forward is the right fit Fast Forward provides a dedicated application page containing the application questions, character limits, and guidance for preparing responses. Applicants should review the questions before beginning the final submission so they can develop coherent and consistent answers across the entire application. Application Review and Use of Artificial Intelligence Fast Forward states that it uses artificial intelligence to assist with reviewing applications. However, applicants should understand that AI does not make the final decision . According to Fast Forward, every application is read and decided by its team. This means applicants should focus on communicating their organization s story, evidence, technology, leadership, and potential impact clearly rather than attempting to optimize their application for an automated system. Interviews Applicants who progress in the selection process will participate in an interview. Fast Forward states that selected applicants may participate in a 40-minute interview with its team. The organization may also contact applicants by email during the application period if clarification is needed. Interviews are expected to take place between October and December 2026 . Final notifications are expected by the end of 2026 . Video Requirements Fast Forward may request video material as part of the application. Applicants can submit a Zoom recording or combine video clips from individual co-founders. This means teams do not necessarily need sophisticated video-production equipment. The most important consideration should be communicating the organization s mission and value proposition clearly and authentically. Reapplying Is Allowed Organizations that apply but are not selected should not necessarily consider the process a dead end. Fast Forward encourages organizations to reapply. The organization notes that some teams apply for multiple years before eventually becoming a strong fit for the programme. This means applicants can use an unsuccessful application as a learning opportunity, strengthen their MVP, demonstrate additional impact, improve their leadership team, develop stronger technology capacity, and apply again in a future cycle. How to Prepare a Strong Application Although Fast Forward evaluates applications holistically, applicants can improve their submission by clearly demonstrating several critical elements. Demonstrate a Real Problem Do not simply state that a problem exists. Explain its scale, consequences, affected populations, and why existing approaches are insufficient. Explain the Technology Clearly The application should make it easy for reviewers to understand what the technology does and how it addresses the identified problem. Avoid unnecessary technical jargon. Prove That an MVP Exists Because an MVP is a hard requirement, applicants should clearly demonstrate that they have progressed beyond an idea. Where possible, explain: What has been built Who is using it What users are saying What has been learned What has changed based on feedback What remains to be developed Show Evidence of Impact Quantitative and qualitative evidence can help demonstrate progress. This might include: Number of users Number of beneficiaries Adoption rates Retention Outcomes Testimonials Partnerships Pilot results Geographic reach Measurable improvements Explain Why You Can Scale Do not simply claim that the organization is scalable. Explain how the technology can reach a much larger population and what resources will be needed to achieve that growth. Highlight the Team Explain why the leadership team is capable of solving the problem. Show the combination of: Technical expertise Sector knowledge Leadership Community understanding Entrepreneurial ability Lived experience Commitment to the mission Explain Why Fast Forward A strong application should also explain why the Accelerator is needed at this particular stage. Applicants should identify the specific gaps Fast Forward can help address, whether those gaps involve fundraising, product strategy, scaling, nonprofit development, technology leadership, impact measurement, or access to networks. Important Considerations for International Applicants International applicants should carefully assess the programme s requirements before applying. Although the Accelerator is global, selected organizations must be able to participate in required in-person activities in San Francisco. Applicants outside the Bay Area should therefore consider: International travel requirements Visa and entry requirements Time-zone differences Availability of at least one co-founder Participation in Tuesday and Thursday sessions Additional weekly meetings Programme homework Attendance at Demo Day Travel logistics Fast Forward provides travel assistance for teams outside the Bay Area, but applicants should still plan carefully for international participation. Who Can Apply? The opportunity is primarily intended for: Early-stage technology nonprofits Nonprofit organizations using software or technology as a central part of their impact model Organizations that already have a minimum viable product Organizations with strong potential for social impact Organizations with software-based solutions capable of scaling U.S.-based nonprofit organizations International nonprofits registered in their respective countries Current organizational leaders, including leaders who are not the original founder Teams with strong technology leadership or a credible plan to build technical capacity Fast Forward does not restrict the Accelerator to a particular race, nationality, or continent. The programme is global and explicitly seeks geographic diversity within its cohorts. Organizations from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, the Middle East, and other regions may therefore be considered, provided they satisfy the programme s requirements. For organizations outside the United States, Fast Forward states that formal U.S. 501(c)(3) status is not required where the organization is properly registered as a nonprofit in its own country. APPLY HERE Who Is Not Eligible? The following organizations may not be suitable for the 2027 Accelerator: Individuals applying without an organization Conventional for-profit startups Organizations without a technology-centered solution Teams that only have an idea and no MVP Organizations still exclusively in the research or concept stage Organizations where software is not central to the impact model Fast Forward specifically focuses on tech nonprofits , so applicants should ensure that the connection between their technology and social impact is clear. How to Apply Applicants should carefully review the official application questions, character limits, and application guidance before preparing their submission. Applicants should also review the Fast Forward website and official programme information for any updates before submitting their application. Visit HERE to learn more about the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator. Application Deadline The deadline to apply for the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT). Applicants are strongly encouraged to submit before the final day to avoid technical problems, time-zone confusion, or incomplete application materials. Conclusion The Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator represents a significant opportunity for early-stage technology nonprofits seeking to move from promising innovation toward sustainable scale. With $25,000+ in philanthropic seed funding , specialized training, mentorship, peer community, fundraising guidance, technology and product support, and access to a broad ecosystem of funders and supporters, the programme goes beyond financial assistance. It is designed to help organizations strengthen the foundations required to become high-impact, scalable technology nonprofits. The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations that have already built an MVP and can demonstrate that their technology addresses a significant social or humanitarian problem. International organizations are welcome, and applicants do not need to be based in San Francisco or hold U.S. 501(c)(3) status, provided they meet the applicable nonprofit requirements. However, applicants should take the programme s time commitment seriously. At least one co-founder must participate in the sessions, the programme includes additional weekly work, and participants must be prepared to attend required in-person activities in San Francisco. For technology nonprofit founders with a functioning MVP, strong social-impact ambitions, and a clear pathway toward scale, this could be an important opportunity to gain the capital, knowledge, relationships, and visibility needed to take their organization to the next level. Application deadline: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. PT. title: 2027 Guggenheim Fellowships in USA and Canada | Funding for Mid-Career Professionals
summary: The John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation has released new, user-friendly resources to help prospective applicants determine whether the Guggenheim Fellowship is the right opportunity for them at this stage of their careers. The Guggenheim Fellowship supports exceptional mid-career professionals across a wide range of fields , including individuals working with or without university affiliations. The Foundation has also published a detailed application guide and video explaining the application process, selection procedure, and materials required. About the Guggenheim Fellowship The Guggenheim Fellowship is designed for established professionals who have demonstrated significant achievement in their fields and have a strong project they are ready to pursue. The Foundation emphasizes that “mid-career” is determined by a candidate’s professional record and output rather than age or institutional affiliation . Recent Fellows have ranged from their late twenties to their late seventies. Applicants should have: A significant and recognized record of achievement in their field. A clear and well-defined project they are ready to undertake. The professional experience and record necessary to complete the proposed project at a high level of excellence. Students and individuals who have not yet established a significant record of achievement are generally not considered strong candidates. Eligibility To be eligible for the 2027 Guggenheim Fellowship, applicants must: Be citizens or permanent residents of the United States or Canada . Be mid-career professionals , with or without university affiliations. Not have previously received a Guggenheim Fellowship . Applicants do not need to hold a university position. Independent professionals without institutional affiliations are considered on an equal footing. The Foundation states that what matters most is the strength of the applicant’s record, the merits of the proposed project, and their readiness to complete it to the highest degree of excellence. How the Selection Process Works Every application is reviewed by hand. The selection process takes more than six months and is conducted by experts selected by the Foundation from among former Guggenheim Fellowship recipients. Each application is assessed in full by two to five reviewers . The strongest applicants are recommended to the interdisciplinary Committee of Selection, which must reach consensus before an applicant advances. Final awards are confirmed by the Foundation’s Board of Trustees. The identities of reviewers and jurors remain confidential. Application Requirements Applicants must complete several sections through the online application portal. Applicant Information Applicants will provide information including: Contact information Project information Addresses Employment history Languages Professional memberships Education Supporting Documents Three major documents are required: Career Narrative – maximum 1,000 words or approximately four pages. Most Significant Works – up to seven works. Statement of Plans – maximum 1,000 words or approximately four pages. Applicants must also provide three references , with a fourth reference permitted. Career Narrative The Career Narrative should explain why the applicant is the right person to complete the proposed project. It should tell the story of the applicant’s career, including what led them to the proposed project, how the project fits into their professional development, and how it connects to their broader goals. The Career Narrative should not simply be a CV or list of accomplishments . Statement of Plans The Statement of Plans should present a clear proposal for a single project that the applicant is prepared to pursue. Applicants should explain: What they want to accomplish and why the project matters. The current stage of the project. What they can realistically accomplish during the six- to twelve-month Fellowship period. Why they are capable of undertaking the proposed work. The statement should be persuasive to both specialists in the applicant’s field and non-specialists serving on the Committee of Selection. Applicants should not include a budget or financial details in the Statement of Plans. References Applicants must provide three references and may provide a fourth . References should be individuals who know the applicant and their work well enough to speak persuasively about their abilities, particularly in relation to the proposed project. References do not have to be Guggenheim Fellows. Applicants are advised to obtain permission from their references before listing them and ensure that they understand the submission timeline. Work Examples Depending on the proposed field, applicants may also need to submit work examples. Requirements vary significantly by field. For example, Fine Arts and Photography applicants may submit up to 20 digital images and/or up to three links to time-based media, while Film-Video applicants can submit links to up to three full-length works. Applicants should carefully review the requirements for their particular field before submitting work examples. Application Document Requirements Supporting documents must: Be in 12-point standard fonts . Be double-spaced . Be submitted as PDFs . Be unsecured and not password protected. Use portrait orientation. Be no larger than 5 MB per document. Deadline September 29, 2026 All required work examples must be submitted or postmarked by September 29, 2026 . Applicants should also make sure they complete the final submission process. Simply completing the application is not enough; applicants must select “ Final Submit Application ” before the deadline for their application to be considered. Important Warning for Applicants The John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation specifically advises applicants to be cautious about external consultants who claim to have special access to the Fellowship selection process. The Foundation does not endorse external consultants and states that individuals who charge a fee do not have inside information about or influence over Fellowship selection. The best way to understand the Fellowship is to use the Foundation’s own application materials, video resources, and official guidance. Applicants with questions are encouraged to contact the Foundation directly. How to Apply The 2027 Guggenheim Fellowship application is available through the official application portal. Application Portal: https://competition.gf.org/signin Applicants can create a new account or use an existing account from the previous competition. Conclusion The Guggenheim Fellowship offers established professionals an opportunity to pursue ambitious work with the support and recognition of one of the most respected fellowship programs in the United States and Canada. If you believe your professional record, proposed project, and achievements make you a strong candidate, take time to study the Foundation’s official materials and prepare your application carefully before the deadline. Discover more fellowship opportunities like this on the OFY Webpage. title: ANeSA 2026 Research Grants: Up to CAD 1.2 Million for Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Projects in Sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Applications are open for the Addressing Neglected Areas of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights in sub-Saharan Africa (ANeSA) 2026 Call for Letters of Interest , a major implementation research funding opportunity supporting innovative, evidence-informed and gender-transformative approaches to neglected sexual and reproductive health and rights challenges across sub-Saharan Africa. The call represents Stage 1 of a two-stage funding process for Cohort 2 of ANeSA Implementation Research Teams. Selected applicants will work on research intended to improve the design, implementation, sustainability and effectiveness of interventions addressing underserved populations and neglected areas of sexual and reproductive health and rights. The initiative is funded by: International Development Research Centre Global Affairs Canada Canadian Institutes of Health Research Up to six grants of as much as CAD 1.2 million each are expected to be awarded. At the first stage, applicants submit a Letter of Interest. Up to 12 applicants will then be invited to proceed to the Full Proposal stage. Successful projects may receive funding for a period of up to 36 months . The deadline for Letters of Interest is August 23, 2026 at 23:59 Eastern Time . About the ANeSA Initiative ANeSA stands for: Addressing Neglected Areas of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights in sub-Saharan Africa. The initiative is focused on improving sexual and reproductive health and rights through implementation research. Its Cohort 2 call seeks research teams capable of studying and strengthening interventions that are: Sustainable Evidence-informed Gender-transformative Relevant to underserved populations Grounded in the realities of sub-Saharan African health systems and communities The opportunity is therefore not simply intended to finance stand-alone academic research. The central emphasis is on implementation research , meaning research that can help understand how interventions are delivered, adapted, scaled, sustained or improved in real-world settings. Projects should contribute to practical improvements in sexual and reproductive health and rights while generating evidence that can inform policy, programming and service delivery. Funding Available The ANeSA Cohort 2 funding opportunity will provide: Up to six grants with a maximum value of: CAD 1.2 million per grant The maximum project duration is: 36 months At the first stage, up to 12 applicants will be shortlisted and invited to submit Full Proposals. This means the competition involves two distinct stages: Letter of Interest Full Proposal Not every Letter of Interest will advance to the second stage. Stage 1: Letter of Interest The current application stage requires eligible Implementation Research Teams to submit a Letter of Interest. The Letter of Interest serves as the first screening stage. Successful applicants from this round will be notified and invited to continue into the Full Proposal process. The deadline is: August 23, 2026 at 23:59 ET Stage 2: Full Proposal Applicants invited to continue will enter a second and more detailed stage. According to the announced timeline: Proposal Development Workshop: February 9–11, 2027 Full Proposal Call Launch: February 12, 2027 Full Proposal Deadline: May 2, 2027 Final Funding Decisions: July 21, 2027 Only invited applicants will proceed to this stage. What Kind of Research Will ANeSA Fund? ANeSA is seeking implementation research addressing neglected sexual and reproductive health and rights priorities. Projects are expected to focus on interventions that are both evidence-informed and gender-transformative. A gender-transformative approach generally means that projects should not simply acknowledge gender inequalities but should seek to address the norms, structures, systems or power relations contributing to unequal health outcomes. The supplied call identifies five priority areas. Applicants must address at least one. Priority Area 1: Family Planning and Contraceptive Services Projects may focus on improving access to: Family planning Modern contraception Contraceptive information Reproductive-health services Appropriate services for underserved populations Research in this area should examine how access, quality, delivery or sustainability can be improved. Potential implementation questions may concern how health systems reach populations that remain excluded from existing family-planning services. Priority Area 2: Safe Abortion and Post-Abortion Care ANeSA supports research related to: Safe abortion care where legally permitted Post-abortion care The call refers to abortion and post-abortion care under the abbreviation APAC . Projects must operate within applicable legal and policy frameworks. Research may examine how appropriate services can be delivered more equitably and effectively, particularly for populations facing barriers to care. Priority Area 3: Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Another major priority is protecting sexual and reproductive health and rights for adolescents. Projects may focus on both rights and access to services. This area may include implementation challenges connected with: Adolescent access to services Youth-friendly care Information Rights Barriers created by institutions, social norms or service-delivery models The call emphasizes not only health services but the broader importance of upholding adolescent SRHR rights . Priority Area 4: Sexual and Gender-Based Violence ANeSA will support research addressing: Prevention of sexual and gender-based violence Improved services for people experiencing sexual and gender-based violence This priority recognizes that effective responses require both prevention and appropriate care. Projects may therefore examine systems, interventions, services and implementation approaches aimed at reducing violence and improving support for affected individuals. Priority Area 5: Strengthening Advocacy for Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights The fifth priority area focuses specifically on: Strengthening advocacy for SRHR. This recognizes that access to rights and services is influenced not only by clinical delivery but also by: Policy Institutions Public debate Community engagement Advocacy Rights frameworks Projects may therefore investigate how advocacy strategies can be implemented more effectively to support improvements in sexual and reproductive health and rights. Focus on Underserved Populations A central element of the call is its focus on underserved populations in sub-Saharan Africa . Applicants should therefore show that the proposed work responds to groups that face meaningful barriers in accessing SRHR rights, services or support. The supplied call does not provide a complete list of populations that qualify as underserved in the summary provided. Applicants should consult the full Call for Letters of Interest for the detailed definitions and requirements. Who Can Lead an Application? The call is open to Implementation Research Teams . The team must be led by: A researcher based in sub-Saharan Africa who is affiliated with: An eligible institution in an eligible country. The Principal Applicant must therefore be affiliated with an organization based in one of the eligible countries listed by the program. The supplied announcement directs applicants to the full Call for Letters of Interest for the detailed: Team composition requirements Institutional eligibility requirements Roles of team members Partnership requirements Additional eligibility conditions Applicants should therefore not rely only on the general call summary when assembling a team. Eligible Countries Principal Applicants must be affiliated with organizations based in one of the following eligible countries in sub-Saharan Africa: Angola Benin Botswana Burkina Faso Burundi Cameroon Central African Republic Chad Congo (Brazzaville) Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kinshasa) Equatorial Guinea Ethiopia Gabon Gambia Ghana Guinea Guinea-Bissau Ivory Coast Kenya Lesotho Liberia Madagascar Malawi Mali Mauritania Mauritius Mozambique Namibia Niger Nigeria Rwanda Senegal Sierra Leone South Africa Eswatini South Sudan Tanzania Togo Uganda Zambia Zimbabwe Countries Subject to Additional Internal Approval The announcement notes that applications from certain countries may be subject to an additional stage of internal approval within IDRC . These countries are: Burkina Faso Burundi Cameroon Central African Republic Chad Democratic Republic of the Congo Ethiopia Gabon Mali Mozambique Niger Nigeria South Sudan Uganda Zimbabwe Applicants from these countries are not described as automatically ineligible. Rather, additional internal review or approval may apply. Project Duration Funded projects may run for: Up to 36 months Applicants should therefore design implementation research that can realistically deliver meaningful results within a three-year timeframe. A strong project is likely to require a clear plan for: Research implementation Partnership management Evidence generation Analysis Knowledge translation Sustainability The precise expectations for work plans and budgets should be verified in the full call documentation. Funding Organizations The ANeSA initiative is funded by three Canadian institutions. International Development Research Centre IDRC supports research and innovation intended to address major development challenges. For this call, it serves as an important institutional platform for supporting locally grounded implementation research in sub-Saharan Africa. Global Affairs Canada Global Affairs Canada contributes to Canada s international development and foreign policy activities. Its participation reinforces the international development dimension of the initiative. Canadian Institutes of Health Research CIHR is one of Canada s principal health-research funding institutions. Its involvement highlights the research and health-systems orientation of the funding opportunity. Two-Stage Selection Process Applicants should understand the full selection timeline before applying. Stage 1: Letters of Interest The current stage is open to eligible Implementation Research Teams. Applicants submit their Letter of Interest by: August 23, 2026 Up to 12 applicants will be selected to move forward. Notification of Stage 1 Results Applicants are scheduled to be notified on: December 18, 2026 Proposal Development Workshop Applicants invited to Stage 2 will participate in a Proposal Development Workshop scheduled for: February 9–11, 2027 This suggests that shortlisted applicants will receive additional preparation before submitting the final proposal. Full Proposal Stage The formal Full Proposal call will launch on: February 12, 2027 The Full Proposal deadline is: May 2, 2027 Final Funding Decision Applicants are expected to be notified of final funding decisions on: July 21, 2027 Complete Timeline Applicants should note the following important dates: Call launched: June 29, 2026 English-focused information webinars: July 15–16, 2026 French-only webinar: July 23, 2026 Deadline for questions to receive a response before submission: August 9, 2026 Letter of Interest deadline: August 23, 2026 Stage 1 result notification: December 18, 2026 Proposal Development Workshop: February 9–11, 2027 Full Proposal Call opens: February 12, 2027 Full Proposal deadline: May 2, 2027 Final funding decisions: July 21, 2027 Information Webinars The initiative organized several information sessions for potential applicants. The sessions held on: July 15, 2026 July 16, 2026 reached maximum capacity. Because those sessions were delivered mainly in English, the organizers offered a third and final session in French on: July 23, 2026 The session ran from: 9:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. Eastern Time and did not include English interpretation. Attendance at a webinar is not required in order to apply. Frequently Asked Questions ANeSA also provides an FAQ page for prospective applicants. The supplied information states that the FAQ is updated regularly. Applicants should therefore consult it when preparing their Letter of Interest, particularly if they have questions about: Eligibility Team composition Funding Institutional requirements Application procedures Proposal development Because the FAQ may be updated during the application period, applicants should review the most recent version before submitting. Contact Information Applicants with questions can contact the ANeSA team at: SRHR-SDSR@idrc.ca The call indicated that questions should ideally have been sent by August 9, 2026 to receive a response before the application deadline. Applicants may still consult the call documents and FAQ for unresolved questions. How to Apply To apply for this funding opportunity, you’ll need an account on SurveyMonkey Apply. If you don’t have an account yet, or need help with your existing one, please refer to their Account setup guide . Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to establish or test their account. APPLY HERE Application Deadline The Letter of Interest deadline is: Sunday, August 23, 2026 at 23:59 Eastern Time This is the deadline for Stage 1. Applicants invited to Stage 2 will face the later Full Proposal deadline of: May 2, 2027 The two deadlines should not be confused. Preparing a Strong Letter of Interest The complete required format should be taken from the official call, but applicants can prepare strategically around the priorities clearly identified in the announcement. 1. Demonstrate Fit With at Least One Priority Area The project must address one or more of ANeSA’s five priorities. Do not describe a broad SRHR project without explaining precisely which priority it addresses. 2. Make the Implementation Research Question Clear ANeSA is specifically seeking implementation research. Applicants should therefore go beyond asking whether an intervention works. They should consider questions such as: How can the intervention be delivered effectively? What prevents implementation? How can it be adapted? What conditions are necessary for sustainability? How can successful interventions be integrated into systems? How can uptake among underserved populations be improved? 3. Show Gender-Transformative Potential The call specifically emphasizes gender-transformative interventions. Applicants should clearly explain how the project responds to gender inequalities rather than treating gender as a superficial variable. 4. Focus on Underserved Populations Describe the population being served and the barriers it faces. The proposal should make clear why the population is underserved and why current systems or interventions have not adequately addressed its needs. 5. Demonstrate Institutional and Team Capacity Because the call targets Implementation Research Teams, applicants should show that their team has the expertise required to deliver the research. Relevant capacity may include: Implementation research SRHR Gender analysis Health systems Community engagement Policy Research methodology The exact required team composition should be confirmed in the full call. 6. Consider Sustainability Early The initiative seeks sustainable interventions. Applicants should therefore explain how the work could remain useful after the project period ends. 7. Connect Research With Evidence Use The strongest projects should not produce evidence that remains isolated within academic publications. Applicants should consider how findings could influence: Health policy Service delivery Programmes Community practice Advocacy Health-system decision-making Why ANeSA Matters Sexual and reproductive health and rights remain closely connected to: Health equity Gender equality Human rights Adolescent wellbeing Maternal health Violence prevention Access to contraception Health-system quality Social and economic development However, significant gaps remain in many contexts, particularly among populations facing multiple forms of exclusion. ANeSA seeks to address those gaps through research focused on implementation , recognizing that evidence about what should work is not enough if effective interventions cannot be delivered equitably, sustainably and at scale. The programme therefore creates an opportunity for researchers and institutions based in sub-Saharan Africa to lead studies directly connected to the realities of communities and health systems in the region. Important Facts at a Glance Initiative: Addressing Neglected Areas of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights in sub-Saharan Africa Abbreviation: ANeSA Current stage: Stage 1 – Letters of Interest Funding: Up to CAD 1.2 million per grant Number of grants: Up to six Stage 2 invitations: Up to 12 applicants Project duration: Up to 36 months Research type: Implementation research Geographic focus: Sub-Saharan Africa Letter of Interest deadline: August 23, 2026 at 23:59 ET Full Proposal deadline for invited applicants: May 2, 2027 Funding decision: July 21, 2027 Contact: SRHR-SDSR@idrc.ca Conclusion The ANeSA 2026 Call for Letters of Interest represents a major funding opportunity for sub-Saharan Africa-based researchers and institutions working to strengthen sexual and reproductive health and rights. With up to six grants worth as much as CAD 1.2 million each , the initiative will support implementation research projects lasting up to three years. Funded work must address at least one of five priorities: Family planning and contraceptive access Safe abortion where legally permitted and post-abortion care Adolescent sexual and reproductive health and rights Sexual and gender-based violence SRHR advocacy Projects should be sustainable, evidence-informed, gender-transformative and focused on underserved populations. The call is specifically designed around locally led research. Principal Applicants must be researchers based in sub-Saharan Africa and affiliated with eligible institutions in one of the listed participating countries. The process begins with a Letter of Interest, after which up to 12 applicants will be invited to develop Full Proposals. Ultimately, up to six teams are expected to receive funding. The Letter of Interest deadline is August 23, 2026 at 23:59 Eastern Time . Applicants should consult the official Call for Letters of Interest and FAQ carefully, particularly for the detailed team-composition, institutional and proposal requirements that are not fully specified in the summary announcement. title: CPHIA 2026 in Addis Ababa: Register for Africa CDC’s 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa
summary: The 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) will take place from 23–27 November 2026 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia , bringing together public health leaders, researchers, policymakers, governments, private-sector actors, innovators, programme implementers, and partners from across Africa and the wider global health community. The conference is co-hosted by the Government of Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) . CPHIA is Africa CDC’s flagship annual public health conference and has grown into an important continental platform for discussing the health challenges facing Africa, sharing scientific evidence and innovations, building partnerships, and turning research into policies, health products, programmes, and practical action. The theme for the 2026 edition is: “Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience.” CPHIA 2026 is expected to feature five days of high-level policy dialogue, scientific sessions, research presentations, innovation showcases, partnership development, networking, awards, exhibitions, and opportunities for organizations to host side events. The official conference website states that more than 30,000 attendees are expected . Researchers also have an opportunity to submit abstracts for presentation at the conference. The current official abstract submission deadline is 15 September 2026 , while early-bird conference registration is scheduled to close on 22 August 2026 . About the International Conference on Public Health in Africa The International Conference on Public Health in Africa, widely known as CPHIA , is a flagship Africa CDC platform bringing together stakeholders across different levels of the health sector. The conference connects: Political leaders Policymakers Scientists Researchers Public health professionals Programme implementers Private-sector representatives Community actors Innovators Development partners Government institutions Global health organizations Its purpose is not simply to provide another scientific conference. CPHIA aims to create a continental space where evidence, political leadership, public-health implementation, financing, innovation, and partnerships can interact. Africa CDC describes the conference as an opportunity for African stakeholders to have open discussions about critical health challenges while sharing scientific breakthroughs and innovations capable of driving positive change. The broader goal is to translate evidence and innovation into health products, tools, policies, and adequately financed programmes. CPHIA 2026 Dates and Location Conference: 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa Dates: 23–27 November 2026 Location: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Host city: Addis Ababa Expected attendance: More than 30,000 delegates Theme: Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience. Addis Ababa is also home to Africa CDC and the African Union headquarters, placing CPHIA 2026 in one of the continent s principal diplomatic and multilateral centres. Why CPHIA Matters for African Public Health The conference has evolved substantially since its first edition in 2021. Africa CDC describes CPHIA as a major platform for African health actors and champions to discuss issues affecting health across the continent and share scientific evidence that can support practical solutions. Its history includes: 2021: Inaugural virtual conference 2022: Kigali, Rwanda 2023: Lusaka, Zambia 2025: Durban, South Africa 2026: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia The inaugural 2021 edition attracted more than 12,000 virtual participants. The 2022 conference in Kigali recorded more than 14,000 in-person and virtual participants, the 2023 event in Lusaka recorded more than 35,000, and the 2025 Durban edition attracted more than 17,000 participants across virtual and physical formats. CPHIA 2026 Mission CPHIA’s mission is centered on bringing together African and international stakeholders to: Share knowledge Build partnerships Catalyse action Strengthen African health security Advance universal health coverage Promote locally driven solutions Strengthen continental solidarity Its vision is of a healthier, prosperous, and more self-reliant Africa supported by stronger health systems, local manufacturing capabilities, and a skilled health workforce. Core Pillars of CPHIA The conference identifies three broad pillars underpinning its work: Science and Innovation Scientific evidence is central to CPHIA. Researchers are given opportunities to present findings and connect scientific knowledge with decision-makers responsible for policy and implementation. Transformative Policies and Action The conference seeks to move discussions beyond identifying problems toward policies and programmes capable of generating change. Political Leadership for Impact Government leadership and political commitment are important components of strengthening health systems and ensuring that research and public-health priorities receive sustained attention and resources. What to Expect at CPHIA 2026 Africa CDC describes CPHIA 2026 as five days of discussions, research presentations, networking, innovation, and collaboration. The conference experience is expected to include six particularly prominent components. 1. High-Level Policy Dialogue CPHIA will bring participants into discussions involving: Heads of State and Government Ministers Global health leaders Members of the diplomatic community This gives the conference a significant policy dimension alongside its scientific programme. 2. Scientific Sessions The conference is expected to feature more than 100 sessions presenting research and innovations designed to contribute to evidence-based policies and action. Researchers whose abstracts are accepted may have opportunities to present their work through oral, poster, or electronic presentation formats. 3. Innovation, Financing and Investment CPHIA 2026 will provide opportunities to showcase health products, technologies, and innovations, with particular attention to African solutions. This reflects the conference theme’s emphasis on reducing health dependency and strengthening the continent’s capacity to own and sustain health solutions. 4. Networking With tens of thousands of delegates expected, CPHIA provides an opportunity to connect with people working across: Government Academia Public health International organizations Health technology Civil society Research Pharmaceutical and health manufacturing Health financing Community health Development cooperation The official conference description specifically emphasizes connections between African participants and the wider global health community. 5. Awards and Recognition CPHIA 2026 will recognize achievements in African health research and innovation, including recognition of young scientists. The abstract programme identifies several awards, including: Best Oral Presentation Best Poster Presentation Young Investigator Award Innovation in Public Health Award 6. Partnerships and Collaboration The conference also seeks to support strategic partnerships that can advance health security and health sovereignty across Africa. CPHIA 2026 Conference Tracks The scientific programme is structured around six major tracks addressing central public-health and health-security issues affecting Africa. Track 1: Elevating Africa as a Leader in a Reformed and Inclusive Global Health Architecture The first track focuses on strengthening Africa’s role in continental and global health priority-setting. It reflects growing debates about: African leadership in global health Governance of global health institutions Representation Equity Decision-making power Health sovereignty International partnerships The emphasis is on positioning Africa not merely as a recipient of global health interventions but as an active leader shaping priorities and solutions. Track 2: Institutionalisation of Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in Africa The second track focuses on strengthening systems for preventing, preparing for, and responding to major health emergencies. The COVID-19 pandemic, Ebola outbreaks, mpox, cholera, and other health emergencies have emphasized the importance of: Surveillance Emergency preparedness Public-health institutions Laboratory capacity Workforce preparedness Cross-border collaboration Rapid response systems CPHIA frames pandemic preparedness as directly connected with continental health security. Track 3: African Stakeholders’ Empowerment and Predictable, Innovative and Blended Financing The third track addresses financing. Its focus is on strengthening self-reliance through innovative and sustainable health financing approaches, including financing connected with universal health coverage. The track reflects the conference’s broader emphasis on moving from dependency toward greater African ownership and financial sustainability. Track 4: Primary Health Care, Digital Transformation and AI-Enabled Health Systems The fourth track addresses one of the fastest-growing areas of contemporary healthcare: the intersection of primary healthcare, digital technology, and artificial intelligence. It explores how digital transformation and AI can support evidence-based healthcare delivery at primary-care level. Potential areas of interest may include: Digital health Artificial intelligence Health data Primary healthcare Digital diagnostics Health information systems Technology-enabled service delivery The official theme emphasizes using digital innovation and AI to strengthen evidence-based primary healthcare. Track 5: Unlocking Opportunities for Local Manufacturing in Africa Local production of health commodities has become an important health-security priority. Track 5 focuses on building Africa’s ability to manufacture the health products it requires. This connects directly with the conference theme of health sovereignty and reduced dependence on external supply chains. Track 6: Climate, Health Security and African Resilience The final major track examines the connections between: Climate change One Health Health security African resilience Climate change increasingly affects disease patterns, food systems, water security, extreme weather, displacement, vector-borne disease, and health-system demand. This track therefore brings environmental and public-health concerns together under a broader resilience framework. CPHIA 2026 Call for Abstracts Researchers have an opportunity to submit research findings that align with the conference tracks. The official CPHIA 2026 call for abstracts opened on: 5 August 2026 The submission deadline is: 15 September 2026 Notification of acceptance is scheduled for: 15 October 2026 Accepted presenters are expected to upload their final presentations by: 30 October 2026 . Important Step Before Submitting an Abstract The conference instructs researchers to complete conference registration first . Once registration is approved, applicants receive confirmation and can then sign in to submit an abstract. Researchers who plan to submit should therefore avoid waiting until the final day to begin registration. Abstract Submission Requirements The official guidelines set a maximum abstract length of: 300 words This excludes the title and author information. The abstract should contain: Background Methods Results Conclusion The abstract title should be concise and no longer than 20 words , and applicants should provide three to five keywords . Research Must Be Original Submitted work should be original and not previously published. Applicants must also: List all authors and affiliations Declare conflicts of interest Indicate their preferred presentation format Presentation preferences can include oral or poster formats. Abstract Review Criteria Submitted research will be assessed according to factors including: Scientific merit Originality Relevance to the CPHIA themes Methodological rigor Potential impact on African public health This means applicants should not merely describe technically strong research. They should also explain why their findings matter for African public health. Abstract Presentation Formats Accepted research may be presented through several formats. Oral Presentation Oral presentations are allocated: 12 minutes for presentation 3 minutes for questions and answers Poster Presentation Posters should be: A0 size 841 × 1189 mm Portrait orientation Dedicated poster sessions will be included during the conference. E-Poster Electronic posters can be displayed digitally on conference screens. The specified format is: PowerPoint Maximum five slides E-posters are expected to remain available during the conference. Important Abstract Rules Researchers should pay attention to several important conditions. The presenting author must register for the conference. Late submissions will not be accepted. Each presenting author may submit a maximum of three abstracts . Accepted abstracts are expected to be included in the conference proceedings. CPHIA 2026 Travel Scholarships The conference homepage identifies a scholarship pathway connected with abstract submission. Researchers submitting high-quality abstracts may be considered for travel scholarships to attend CPHIA 2026 . The current conference participation page lists 15 September 2026 as the relevant deadline. However, the public conference information currently available does not provide detailed scholarship values, complete eligibility criteria, or a guarantee that every accepted abstract author will receive support. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that abstract acceptance automatically means funded travel. Researchers interested in travel support should monitor the official CPHIA website for additional scholarship guidance. CPHIA 2026 Registration Timeline The official abstract page currently lists the following registration dates: Early-bird registration opens: 3 August 2026 Early-bird registration deadline: 22 August 2026 Regular registration opens: 23 August 2026 Conference: 23–27 November 2026. Because early-bird registration is time-sensitive, participants planning to attend should complete registration promptly if they wish to use the early registration period. The publicly accessible registration page retrieved for this article does not display complete fee information, so applicants should confirm current prices directly through the official registration portal rather than relying on unofficial sources. CPHIA 2026 Side Events Organizations can also apply to organize a side event during conference week. Side events are intended as satellite sessions that complement the main conference programme and give organizations an opportunity to engage ministers, researchers, partners, and other public-health stakeholders. The current timeline is: Applications open: 7 August 2026 Deadline: 15 September 2026 Review and notification: 15 October 2026 Final programme details due: 30 October 2026 Side event week: 23–27 November 2026. Side Event Requirements Organizations should submit a clear proposal describing: Session theme Target audience Expected outcomes Applicants must also demonstrate organizational capacity to host and promote their event. The proposed side event should align with CPHIA and broader African public-health priorities. Exhibition Opportunities Organizations developing health products, technologies, services, research, and innovations can apply for exhibition space. CPHIA describes the exhibition programme as a platform for organizations to showcase solutions to scientists, policymakers, health leaders, and advocates. Key exhibition dates include: Applications open: 7 August 2026 Application deadline: 15 September 2026 Notification of approval: 15 October 2026 Payment deadline: 31 October 2026 Booth setup begins: 1 November 2026 Exhibition days: 23–27 November 2026. At the time the official exhibition page was reviewed, specific active exhibition packages had not yet been published. Who Should Consider Exhibiting? The exhibition component may be particularly relevant for organizations seeking to: Showcase health innovations Present products and services Reach decision-makers Develop partnerships Build visibility across African Union Member States Connect with health ministries, researchers, and industry leaders CPHIA emphasizes Pan-African visibility and access to a high-level public-health audience. Corporate Sponsorship Opportunities CPHIA 2026 also provides corporate sponsorship options. The conference lists seven partnership categories, including: Platinum Gold Silver Bronze Targeted sponsorship Customized sponsorship Other negotiated arrangements Published sponsorship values include: Platinum: USD 250,000 Gold: USD 150,000 Silver: USD 75,000 Bronze: USD 35,000–50,000 Other packages are negotiable. Corporate sponsorship is reviewed on a rolling basis. CPHIA 2026 Speakers The conference is expected to bring together major African voices in public health, policy, research, and innovation. One confirmed keynote speaker listed on the official website is Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director General of Africa CDC . The conference speaker page also invites experts to participate through: Research abstract submissions Session or workshop proposals Panel discussions Satellite or side events The broader scientific direction is supported by a Scientific Committee composed of researchers and public-health leaders from institutions across Africa and beyond. Awards for Researchers Researchers participating through the abstract pathway may be considered for conference recognition. The current call lists: Best Oral Presentation Best Poster Presentation Young Investigator Award Innovation in Public Health Award These awards create an additional opportunity for early-career and established researchers to gain visibility for work with strong relevance to African public health. Addis Ababa as the Host City Addis Ababa will host the conference from 23–27 November.
